questions.question: What is the primary conceptual role of a basis transform (e.g., Fourier, DCT, Hadamard) in a learning pipeline from a signal-processing perspective?
questions.choice_A: It re-expresses data in coordinates where important structure becomes disentangled or sparse.
questions.choice_B: It increases the dimensionality to avoid overfitting by the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma.
questions.choice_C: It removes all noise by thresholding high-frequency components to zero.
questions.choice_D: It guarantees linear separability of any dataset.

questions.question: Why is sparsity in a transform domain considered an advantageous inductive bias for learning from natural data?
questions.choice_A: Because sparse models necessarily have fewer parameters than dense models.
questions.choice_B: Because sparse representations concentrate information in few coefficients, aiding generalization and sample efficiency.
questions.choice_C: Because sparse coefficients eliminate the need for regularization.
questions.choice_D: Because sparsity only arises when the data is noise-free.

questions.question: Which statement best explains why the Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) is widely used for images?
questions.choice_A: It is invariant to translations and rotations of the image.
questions.choice_B: It computes edges directly by local differencing.
questions.choice_C: It compacts most image energy into low-frequency coefficients, making image content parsimonious to represent.
questions.choice_D: It is a nonlinear transform that adapts to every image individually.

questions.question: In terms of inductive bias, how does a global transform like the discrete Fourier transform differ from a localized transform like a wavelet transform?
questions.choice_A: Fourier emphasizes spatial locality while wavelets emphasize global periodicity.
questions.choice_B: Both are equally localized in space and frequency.
questions.choice_C: Wavelets assume global stationarity; Fourier assumes local stationarity.
questions.choice_D: Fourier favors global periodic structure; wavelets favor localized, multiscale structure.

questions.question: How do structured linear operators encode priors about natural data?
questions.choice_A: By constraining the hypothesis class to functions compatible with assumed symmetries or regularities (e.g., shift invariance).
questions.choice_B: By expanding the hypothesis class to include all possible functions.
questions.choice_C: By enforcing nonlinearity through element-wise activations.
questions.choice_D: By randomizing weights to average out biases.

questions.question: Why can convolution be viewed as a structured linear map with a useful inductive bias?
questions.choice_A: It reduces model depth, eliminating the need for multiple layers.
questions.choice_B: It enforces weight sharing and shift equivariance, reflecting the prior that patterns can appear anywhere.
questions.choice_C: It enforces orthogonality of filters by construction.
questions.choice_D: It guarantees perfect reconstruction of inputs.

questions.question: What property of circulant matrices connects them to convolution and fast transforms?
questions.choice_A: They are always sparse, with only a few nonzero entries.
questions.choice_B: They diagonalize under the Hadamard transform for any signal length.
questions.choice_C: They are diagonalized by the discrete Fourier transform, enabling fast multiplication via FFT.
questions.choice_D: They are necessarily low-rank for natural images.

questions.question: Which description best captures the inductive bias of the Hadamard transform when used as a feature map?
questions.choice_A: Preference for narrowband periodic signals with long coherence times.
questions.choice_B: Adaptation to local singularities through variable bandwidth atoms.
questions.choice_C: Explicit modeling of spatially varying frequencies via chirps.
questions.choice_D: Promotion of piecewise-constant structure due to its binary ±1 basis patterns and energy spreading.

questions.question: How does energy compaction relate to generalization in models that use fixed transforms for feature extraction?
questions.choice_A: By concentrating informative content in a few coefficients, it reduces effective dimensionality and can lower variance.
questions.choice_B: By spreading information evenly across coefficients, it avoids bias.
questions.choice_C: By guaranteeing that low-energy coefficients contain only noise.
questions.choice_D: By ensuring the features are linearly separable.

questions.question: What is a key reason fast transforms (e.g., FFT, FWHT) are effective for scalable kernel approximation?
questions.choice_A: They approximate any kernel with zero error if enough features are used.
questions.choice_B: They enable structured random features that are cheap to multiply and preserve key statistical properties.
questions.choice_C: They avoid randomness, thereby reducing variance in the estimator.
questions.choice_D: They convert nonlinear kernels into linear kernels without approximation.

questions.question: Random Fourier Features approximate which class of kernels and why is the Fourier transform relevant?
questions.choice_A: Polynomial kernels; because polynomials have Fourier series.
questions.choice_B: Linear kernels; because the Fourier transform linearizes dot products.
questions.choice_C: Shift-invariant kernels; because Bochner's theorem links them to Fourier transforms of probability measures.
questions.choice_D: Graph kernels; because graphs have spectral Laplacians.

questions.question: In the context of localized transforms, what is the main benefit of time-frequency windows or multiscale atoms for nonstationary signals?
questions.choice_A: They force all high frequencies to zero, denoising the signal.
questions.choice_B: They ensure exact sparsity for any signal.
questions.choice_C: They remove phase information while retaining magnitude.
questions.choice_D: They capture transient, localized phenomena that global bases smear across many coefficients.

questions.question: Why does imposing transform-domain sparsity act like a form of regularization in learning?
questions.choice_A: It constrains solutions to those explainable by few active basis functions, reducing overfitting risk.
questions.choice_B: It increases the number of parameters to better fit the data.
questions.choice_C: It eliminates the need for validation data.
questions.choice_D: It guarantees zero training error.

questions.question: How does the assumption of shift invariance in natural images motivate convolutional architectures over fully connected ones?
questions.choice_A: Fully connected networks cannot represent shift-invariant functions.
questions.choice_B: Convolution enforces parameter sharing across spatial positions, reflecting that features recur regardless of location.
questions.choice_C: Convolution removes the need for nonlinearities.
questions.choice_D: Fully connected layers inherently violate causality.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between Fourier and DCT bases that explains DCT's practical advantage in image compression?
questions.choice_A: DCT basis functions are adaptive to each image.
questions.choice_B: Fourier uses real sinusoids while DCT uses complex exponentials.
questions.choice_C: DCT uses only real cosines and effectively handles boundary conditions to reduce blocking/edge artifacts and compact energy.
questions.choice_D: Fourier inherently loses phase, while DCT preserves it.

questions.question: How can structured transforms improve the bias-variance trade-off in models trained on limited data?
questions.choice_A: By increasing variance and bias simultaneously to avoid underfitting.
questions.choice_B: By ensuring zero bias through perfect basis alignment.
questions.choice_C: By reducing bias only, while variance remains unchanged.
questions.choice_D: By injecting priors that reduce variance (via parameter tying or dimensionality reduction) at acceptable bias levels.

questions.question: Why are fast transforms attractive as first-layer feature extractors in large-scale models?
questions.choice_A: They provide a fixed, low-cost mapping that can reveal sparse/structured features aligned with natural signal statistics.
questions.choice_B: They remove the need for any subsequent learning.
questions.choice_C: They guarantee robustness to adversarial perturbations.
questions.choice_D: They automatically adapt to the training distribution without constraints.

questions.question: What is the relationship between convolution in the time domain and multiplication in the frequency domain, and why does it matter for learning?
questions.choice_A: They are unrelated; convolution is nonlinear while multiplication is linear.
questions.choice_B: Convolution corresponds to pointwise multiplication in the frequency domain, simplifying analysis and enabling fast implementations.
questions.choice_C: Convolution corresponds to addition in the frequency domain, aiding denoising.
questions.choice_D: Convolution is identical to correlation in both domains.

questions.question: How do structural assumptions embedded in transforms influence out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization?
questions.choice_A: They guarantee OOD robustness by construction.
questions.choice_B: They never help OOD since biases overfit the training set.
questions.choice_C: They can help when OOD shifts preserve the assumed structure (e.g., shift invariance), but can hurt when the assumptions are violated.
questions.choice_D: They only affect training speed, not generalization.

questions.question: Which statement best characterizes the role of orthogonality in classical transforms used for feature extraction?
questions.choice_A: Orthogonality ensures the transform is nonlinear and hence expressive.
questions.choice_B: Orthogonality guarantees that all information is compressed into the first coefficient.
questions.choice_C: Orthogonality provides energy preservation and decorrelation under certain models, which aids analysis and denoising.
questions.choice_D: Orthogonality prevents overfitting regardless of dataset size.

questions.question: When using structured random projections (e.g., subsampled randomized Hadamard transforms) in learning pipelines, what is the main benefit over dense Gaussian projections?
questions.choice_A: They achieve lower approximation error in all cases.
questions.choice_B: They allow fast multiply and memory efficiency while approximately preserving distances, enabling scalable dimensionality reduction.
questions.choice_C: They remove the need for any randomization in the model.
questions.choice_D: They produce exactly sparse outputs with no distortion.
